notes.title: Start here: one delivery, from the form to the store
notes.body:
This pack studies one small change in RouteIQ, a Next.js demo for delivery drivers: proof of delivery (method, recipient name, note, photo) now passes a runtime check before it is saved in the Zustand store and in localStorage.

Suggested reading order:

1. `astraupskill/README.md`, "How to use the repository". It lists the source files in the order to open them and suggests a two-column notebook: "input and policy" on the left, "state and consumer" on the right.
2. `astraupskill/02-CONCEPTS.md`: the vocabulary (sanitizer, command guard, boundary, invariant). Most quizzes come from here.
3. `src/lib/deliveryValidation.ts`: about 50 lines. Read it slowly; every rule in the concepts guide is one line here.
4. `src/store/useAppStore.ts` around `recordFailure` (line 940): see where the check sits relative to the first state change.
5. `astraupskill/04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md`: the tests, the check order, and where to look when something breaks.

Keep asking one question while you read: if this value is bad, is it dropped quietly or is the whole action refused?

excerpts.quote: Open the source in this order: `src/lib/types.ts` defines the domain; `src/components/driver/DeliverySheet.tsx` collects user input; `src/store/useAppStore.ts` owns mutations and persistence; `src/lib/deliveryValidation.ts` is the new runtime boundary; `src/components/driver/report.ts` consumes events.

readMore.why: The course overview: what changed, the suggested pace, and the limits of the localStorage demo.
A map of the request path from the driver form to persisted state.

notes.title: Why a TypeScript type is not a runtime check
notes.body:
TypeScript checks your code while you write and compile it. When the app runs in the browser the types are gone: the JavaScript that actually runs has no idea what `DeliveryProofInput` was. So a type only helps the developers who call the function from typed code. It cannot inspect a value that arrives some other way, for example from plain JavaScript or from data saved in localStorage by an older version of the app.

That is why the repo adds real code that looks at the value while the program runs. A function like `isDeliveryMethod` takes `unknown` and returns true only for one of four known strings. The `value is DeliveryMethod` return type is the "narrowing" part from the glossary: after the check returns true, TypeScript lets you treat the value as the specific type.

When you read the store, look for the places where an outside value is first used and ask: which runtime check ran before this line?

excerpts.quote: const METHODS = new Set<DeliveryMethod>(['handed', 'door', 'neighbour', 'desk']);
export function isDeliveryMethod(value: unknown): value is DeliveryMethod { return typeof value === 'string' && METHODS.has(value as DeliveryMethod); }
*Runtime guard*: a check that runs on real data (`isDeliveryMethod`), as opposed to a compile-time type that is erased.

readMore.why: The glossary: runtime guard, boundary, narrowing, data URL and proof/event parity in one paragraph.

notes.title: Two policies: clean up optional data, refuse bad commands
notes.body:
The concepts guide separates two jobs that beginners often mix up.

A **sanitizer** takes any value and keeps only the parts it understands. It never fails; at worst it hands back less than it was given. `sanitizeDeliveryProof` is one: it starts from an empty object and copies a field in only when that field passes its check.

A **command guard** decides whether an action is allowed to happen at all. If the guard says no, the action stops before it changes anything. The concepts guide shows the shape in three lines of code: tolerant cleaning first, then a guard that can return early, then the state change "only after the guard".

Also look at `cleanText` in the validator: it shows what happens to a string field in three steps (is it a string, trim it, cut it to a maximum length). Work out by hand what it returns for a few odd inputs before you try the quizzes.

excerpts.quote: Think of a sanitizer as a projection from a large unknown space into a small accepted space. It cannot add a required timestamp or decide authorization. A command guard is different: it decides whether a state transition is allowed.
const safe = sanitizeDeliveryProof(input); // optional fields may disappear
function cleanText(value: unknown, maxLength: number): string | undefined { if (typeof value !== 'string') return undefined; const cleaned = value.trim();

readMore.why: One paragraph on why keeping the two policies apart makes callers predictable.

notes.title: Why a bad note is dropped but a bad reason is refused
notes.body:
**Key: the note is optional proof, while the reason defines what the event means.**

A delivery note is extra detail. If it is malformed, the sanitizer removes it and the delivery is still a real, useful event. A failure reason is different: it is the meaning of a "failed" event, and the reports count by it. If the store accepted an unknown reason, or replaced it with a guess, the log would contain an outcome nobody actually recorded. So `recordFailure` checks the reason first and returns `false` before any state changes.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Notes validated in the UI form*: the point of the change is that the store checks input itself, whoever calls it.
- *TypeScript narrowing in setStopStatus*: types are erased at runtime; the reason is about the meaning of the event, not the compiler.
- *localStorage budget*: the storage budget is about photo bytes, not reason strings.

excerpts.quote: A failure reason controls the meaning of an event, so `recordFailure` rejects an unknown reason with `false`. This distinction avoids inventing a fake reason while keeping a delivery usable when an optional note is malformed.
if (!state.stops.some((s) => s.id === stopId) || !isFailureReason(reason)) return false;

notes.title: When the photo-budget test fails, inspect, do not loosen
notes.body:
**Key: inspect the retained photo length against PHOTO_BUDGET_BYTES.**

A failing test is information. The guide says to look at the actual numbers: how long is the photo the store kept, and how does the store compare it with `PHOTO_BUDGET_BYTES`? That tells you whether the code or the test fixture is wrong.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Relax the data URL regex*: the guide says the opposite, "do not weaken the validator to accommodate an invalid fixture". The regex is the format check; loosening it lets bad data in for real users too.
- *Skip the test on Windows*: for Windows-only failures the guide asks you to keep the command, exit code and report file so a reviewer can tell environment trouble from a regression. Skipping hides the evidence.
- *Raise PHOTO_BUDGET_BYTES*: that changes product behaviour to make one test pass, and the budget test is built from the constant, so it would just follow the new value.

excerpts.quote: If the store test fails at the photo budget, inspect the actual retained photo length and the `PHOTO_BUDGET_BYTES` comparison; do not weaken the validator to accommodate an invalid fixture.

notes.title: An https photo URL comes back as an empty object
notes.body:
**Key: an empty object, with the https photo dropped as not a data URL.**

Follow `sanitizeDeliveryProof` line by line. The input is an object, so it does not return early. There is no method, name or note, so nothing is copied for those. The photo is a string, so it is trimmed to `https://example.test/x.png`. Then it must match a regex that starts with `^data:image`. An https address does not, so `output.photo` is never set and the function returns `{}`. The test file asserts exactly this with `toEqual({})`.

Why the others are wrong:
- *`{ photo: undefined }`*: the code only assigns `output.photo` inside `if (isDataUrl)`, so the key is never created.
- *It throws*: a sanitizer drops what it does not accept; nothing here throws.
- *Trimmed https URL kept*: trimming happens, but trimming only removes spaces. It cannot turn another scheme into a data URL.

excerpts.quote: const isDataUrl = typeof photo === 'string' && /^data:image\/[a-z0-9.+-]+;base64,[a-z0-9+/]+=*$/i.test(photo); if (isDataUrl) { output.photo = photo; }
expect(sanitizeDeliveryProof({ photo: ' https://example.test/x.png ' })).toEqual({});

notes.title: What a good test of a refused recordFailure checks
notes.body:
**Key: the false return plus no side effects, with stop and log unchanged.**

A refusal has two parts: the function says no (`false`), and nothing changed. A test that only checks the return value would still pass if a future edit moved the guard after `setStopStatus`: the function would return `false` but the stop would already be marked failed. So the guide says to record the stop and the log length before the call and compare them after.

Why the others are wrong:
- *isFailureReason called exactly once*: that is an implementation detail; the guide says to avoid asserting helper call counts, because a correct refactor could break the test.
- *Only the false return*: this misses the side-effect half explained above.
- *Status failed with reason 'Other'*: that describes the store inventing a reason, which is exactly what the design forbids.

excerpts.quote: A good regression test asserts both the returned result and the absence of side effects for rejection. In a store test, snapshot the stop and log lengths before an invalid call and compare them afterward. Avoid asserting implementation details such as helper call counts.

readMore.why: Exercise 7 moves the guard after setStopStatus so you can watch the store test fail.

notes.title: recordFailure with 'Lost' changes nothing
notes.body:
**Key: it returns false, leaving the stop pending with no event appended.**

The known reasons are a fixed set: 'No one home', 'Wrong address', 'Damaged', 'Other'. 'Lost' is not in it, so `isFailureReason('Lost')` is false. The very first check in `recordFailure` returns `false` at line 942, before `setStopStatus` at line 946 and before the `appendEvent` call. Nothing after the `return` runs, so the stop keeps its old status and the log gets no event. The concepts guide states the rule: an invalid stop or reason must leave state unchanged.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Pending but a 'failed' event logged*: the event is appended after the guard, so it never runs.
- *Marked failed with no reason*: `setStopStatus` is also after the guard.
- *Marked failed with 'Other'*: replacing the reason would be "inventing a fake reason", which the design avoids.

excerpts.quote: const REASONS = new Set<FailureReason>(['No one home', 'Wrong address', 'Damaged', 'Other']);
if (!state.stops.some((s) => s.id === stopId) || !isFailureReason(reason)) return false;
An invalid stop or reason must leave state unchanged.

notes.title: A note of only spaces becomes no note at all
notes.body:
**Key: nothing, as trimming turns a blank note into an absent field.**

`cleanText` trims the string first. Five spaces trimmed is the empty string `''`. Then `return cleaned ? cleaned.slice(0, maxLength) : undefined`: an empty string counts as false in JavaScript, so the function returns `undefined`. Back in `sanitizeDeliveryProof`, `if (note) output.note = note;` does not run, so the result simply has no `note` key. The guide calls this normalization: whitespace-only values become absent.

Why the others are wrong:
- *A placeholder note*: a sanitizer cannot add data that was not there; it only keeps or drops.
- *The original spaces*: trimming runs before the length cut, so the spaces are removed.
- *An empty string*: `cleanText` returns `undefined` for an empty result, and the `if (note)` check skips it, so no empty string is stored.

excerpts.quote: const cleaned = value.trim(); return cleaned ? cleaned.slice(0, maxLength) : undefined;
if (note) output.note = note;
Trimming is normalization: it makes whitespace-only values absent.

notes.title: What the delivery validator says it does not do
notes.body:
**Key: make two browser tabs' writes transactional.**

The concepts guide lists the validator's limits on purpose: it does not prove authorization, does not decode image bytes, and does not make two tabs transactional. Two tabs writing to the same localStorage is a coordination problem (the README calls it last-writer-wins). A function that checks one value at a time cannot solve that; the guide says it needs server or coordination design.

Why the others are wrong (all three are things the validator does do):
- *Reject a failure reason outside the known vocabulary*: `isFailureReason` plus the guard in `recordFailure`.
- *Drop a photo that is not an image data URL*: the data URL regex in `sanitizeDeliveryProof`.
- *Trim and bound free-text proof fields*: `cleanText` trims and cuts names to 120 and notes to 500 characters.

excerpts.quote: This validator does not prove authorization, decode image bytes, or make two tabs transactional. Those require server or coordination design beyond this browser demo.
RouteIQ still has last-writer-wins cross-tab behavior, browser storage quotas, and no authentication.

notes.title: Why the typed proof parameter still needs a sanitizer
notes.body:
**Key: types are erased, so JS callers or old storage can pass any value.**

`proof?: DeliveryProofInput` is checked only when TypeScript compiles your code. In the browser the annotation no longer exists. A plain JavaScript caller, a browser extension, or an object restored from localStorage that an older version saved can hand the store anything. The sanitizer runs on the real value at runtime, so it protects every caller.

Why the others are wrong:
- *zustand converts every argument to a string*: nothing in the store does this; the sanitizer checks objects and strings as they are.
- *Next.js strips types only in production*: types are removed in every build, development included; that is how TypeScript works, not a production setting.
- *The compiler cannot check optional parameters*: it can; the guide says the type "helps a developer pass the right fields". The problem is only the callers the compiler never sees.

excerpts.quote: A TypeScript type is erased at runtime. `proof?: DeliveryProofInput` helps a developer pass the right fields, but it cannot stop a plain JavaScript caller or a value restored from old localStorage.
Keep persisted proof data bounded and structurally safe even when a caller * is JavaScript, a stale form, or a browser extension rather than TypeScript.

notes.title: The 120 and 500 character limits are a storage policy
notes.body:
**Key: a storage policy against unbounded localStorage writes.**

RouteIQ keeps everything in the browser's localStorage, which has a size quota. If one note could be any length, a single paste could bloat the saved state. The guide names the purpose directly: length bounds are a storage policy that protects the demo from accidental unbounded writes. In code they are two constants, `MAX_NAME_LENGTH = 120` and `MAX_NOTE_LENGTH = 500`, applied by `cleanText` with `slice`.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Authorization for dispatchers*: the guide says the validator "does not prove authorization"; the limits apply to every caller equally.
- *A UX rule for the phone screen*: the guide gives no screen-size reason; the limits protect storage.
- *Blocking script injection*: cutting a string to 500 characters does not make its content safe; it only makes it shorter.

excerpts.quote: Length bounds are a storage policy: they protect a localStorage-backed demo from accidental unbounded writes.
const MAX_NAME_LENGTH = 120; const MAX_NOTE_LENGTH = 500;

notes.title: Why the budget test derives its photo from the constant
notes.body:
**Key: so changing the constant cannot silently make the test meaningless.**

The test wants a photo that sits just around the budget. With a hard-coded `1_499_960`, the number only means "just under the budget" while `PHOTO_BUDGET_BYTES` has its current value. If someone later changed the budget, the literal would no longer be near the edge, and the test would keep passing while testing nothing interesting. Writing `PHOTO_BUDGET_BYTES - 40` ties the fixture to the rule it tests, so it moves when the rule moves.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Runs faster with a smaller photo*: the size is about the same; only the way it is written changed.
- *Vitest cannot compare numbers above a million*: there is no such limit, and the old test ran with that literal.
- *The literal exceeded the localStorage quota*: the guide gives one reason only, keeping the test meaningful.

excerpts.quote: The store test for the budget builds its oversized photo from `PHOTO_BUDGET_BYTES - 40` so that changing the constant cannot silently make the test meaningless; before the fix pass it hard-coded `1_499_960`.

notes.title: Stop changed but no event: start at the setter
notes.body:
**Key: the store setter and appendEvent.**

Use the symptom to pick the layer. The stop's status did change, so the input passed the checks and the store did run. The missing piece is the event in the log, and events are written by the store's `set` call through `appendEvent`. So that is the first place to look. The guide gives this as a pair of rules: stop changed but no event, inspect the setter and `appendEvent`; event present but report wrong, inspect `report.ts`.

Why the others are wrong:
- *report.ts and the event type*: that is for the opposite symptom, when the event exists but the report reads it wrongly.
- *sanitizeDeliveryProof*: a bad note is dropped quietly and the delivery still goes through, so it cannot explain a missing event.
- *The Next.js build*: a build problem from a server module importing the store shows up as a failed build, not as a missing log entry at runtime.

excerpts.quote: If the stop changes but no event appears, inspect the store setter and `appendEvent`. If the event appears but a report is wrong, inspect `report.ts` and the event type. If a build fails only in Next, check whether a server module imported a browser-only store.
deliveryLog: appendEvent(s.deliveryLog, event),
